::: {.atlas-lead}
Every federal law, regulation and guideline, and every international treaty,
that the Supreme Court publishes in consolidated form is one point on this map. Two instruments sit close together
when the texts nearest to their excerpts live in the same places, so that the
organic laws of the public universities, for instance, land beside one
another whatever words they happen to use, and the treaties gather in a region
of their own.
:::

## Where the instruments come from

The texts come from the legislative database of the Supreme Court of Justice of
the Nation ([legislacion.scjn.gob.mx<wbr>/consulta](https://legislacion.scjn.gob.mx/consulta/home)),
which keeps for every instrument a table of its reforms and serves the
consolidated text of the instrument as it stood after each one. The project
reads the database through the Court's own search service, which gives every
instrument a stable identifier. The *Diario Oficial de la Federación* remains
the official source of legal text, and the consolidated versions of the Court
are an editorial product.

The 315 laws, which include the codes and the Constitution, are published as the
[`scjn-leyes`](https://github.com/INGEOTEC/LegalIA/releases/tag/scjn-leyes)
corpus, and the [Federal Laws page](leyes.ipynb) describes it in full. The list of
federal laws was seeded from the catalogue of federal legislation that the Cámara
de Diputados publishes ([LeyesBiblio](https://www.diputados.gob.mx/LeyesBiblio/),
316 instruments), which gave each law its name and its abbreviation. Each law was
then searched by its name in the Court's database and resolved by the identifier
the Court gives it, and never by the rank of the search, because the Court's
search can return a wrong document for a name. Its whole reform table was crawled,
which gives one dated text for every reform, 3,707 texts in all.

The Court's search has no way of listing everything, so the 1,087 regulations
([`scjn-reglamentos`](https://github.com/INGEOTEC/LegalIA/releases/tag/scjn-reglamentos))
and the 163 guidelines
([`scjn-lineamientos`](https://github.com/INGEOTEC/LegalIA/releases/tag/scjn-lineamientos))
were found through a set of phrase searches. These did not use the search form of
the site but the search service behind it, which accepts the scope and the
category of the instruments as part of each request even where the form does not
offer them as choices, and which answers every instrument together with its
category, as the listing of the site shows. Each phrase was sent to the service
for the federal scope and for the category REGLAMENTO or LINEAMIENTOS, the
service answered in pages, and every page was read to the end, so that the union
of the results of the phrases is the list of candidates. The phrases
for the regulations were `reglamento`, `de`, `a`, `la`, `y`, `para` and `el`, and
those for the guidelines were `lineamientos`, `lineamiento`, `de`, `a`, `la`, `y`,
`para` and `el`. Besides the word of the category, the short common words are
there so that an instrument of the category whose title does not contain that word
is still reached. To these were added the instruments that the Court files under
another category but whose own reform table has a row of that category, which were
looked for among the hits of one phrase, `reglamento` for the regulations and
`lineamientos` for the guidelines, and which rescued 6 regulations and 4
guidelines. Because the Court reissues a regulation under a new identifier
instead of reforming it, these two corpora are keyed by that identifier and not
by name. For 5 regulations and 37 guidelines the Court serves no text at all, so
they belong to the corpora but cannot appear on the map.

The treaties were found in a different way, because the Court does not file a
treaty as a federal instrument but gives it a scope of its own, *Tratados
Internacionales*. A treaty is therefore any instrument of that scope, whatever
its category, since the category of a treaty is as likely to be a convention, an
agreement or a protocol as a treaty in the strict sense, and a list of categories
would have left hundreds of them out. The scope was read in pages through the same
search service, with a union of the phrases `tratado`, `convenio`, `convencion`,
`arreglo`, `carta`, `declaracion`, `pacto`, `protocolo`, `acuerdo`, `de`, `a`,
`la`, `y`, `para` and `el`, which serve only to page through the scope and do not
decide whether an instrument belongs to it. This found 1,455 treaties
([`scjn-tratados`](https://github.com/INGEOTEC/LegalIA/releases/tag/scjn-tratados)),
and for 82 of them the Court serves no text, so that 1,373 appear on the map.

The map uses the newest consolidated text of every instrument, one per
instrument. Since regulations are reissued, several regulations or guidelines
share one name, and the map keeps only the most recently issued of them, names
being compared after folding accents, case and whitespace and only within a
collection, so that laws are never grouped, and neither are treaties, since no two
of the 1,373 share a name. This leaves 315 laws, 863 regulations, 125 guidelines
and 1,373 treaties, which are 2,676 instruments once 220 have been dropped (219
regulations and 1 guideline). The current text of each of them is then divided
into excerpts, as the section on what is compared describes.

## How to read the map

::: {.fronts}
::: {.front}
### A point

A point is one law, regulation, guideline or treaty. Its area is proportional to its
counted excerpts, that is, to the number of articles and other pieces of text
into which it is divided and which are compared with those of other
instruments (its headings and transitory articles are not). Its colour is its
collection, blue for laws, green for regulations, magenta for guidelines and yellow for
treaties.
:::
::: {.front}
### Distance

Two instruments sit together when the closest texts of their excerpts live in
the same places, and not when they use the same words. The map is therefore a
picture of where federal law borrows from itself and repeats itself.
:::
::: {.front}
### The numbers

Each excerpt, a block of text cut from an instrument whatever its role, was
matched to the single closest text outside its own instrument. A match shared
by *m* instruments gives 1/*m* to each of them, so that every excerpt that
counts adds up to one.
:::
:::

Searching for an instrument or clicking a point fills the panel with the five
instruments to which its excerpts are closest, together with the number of its
counted excerpts that went to each, and with the five instruments whose
excerpts point at it most often. Lines on the map join the selected instrument
to its five closest instruments and are numbered as in the panel, and a name in
the panel selects that instrument, so that the relations can be followed from
one instrument to the next. The map can be zoomed by scrolling or pinching and
moved by dragging, and the selection is cleared by pressing Escape or by
clicking an empty spot. The collection buttons under the map show one
collection at a time.

Each weight under *Closest instruments* is itself a button. It opens a table
of the excerpts behind that number, each beside the closest text the other
instrument has, both in full, together with how similar the two are and how
much the match adds to the weight, which is 1, or 1/*m* when the matching text
is shared by *m* instruments.

## What is compared

An excerpt is a piece of an instrument's text that is set beside those of the
other instruments, and it is an article, whatever its length, the preamble, the
closing text, a heading or a block of loose text. The text that represents an
article is its own text as it stands in the consolidated law, with its number
label and nothing added, so that neither the name of the law nor the heading of
the chapter in which the article sits becomes part of what is compared. Article
1 of the *LEY que crea la Universidad Autónoma Chapingo* is therefore
represented by

> **ARTICULO 1o.-** Se crea la Universidad Autónoma Chapingo como organismo
> descentralizado del Estado, con personalidad jurídica, patrimonio propio y sede
> de gobierno en Chapingo, Estado de México.

and not by the heading of the chapter above it, **CAPITULO I** De su
Naturaleza, Objetivos y Medios, which is left out.

Exactly this text is what the three methods receive. Each Qwen3-Embedding model
reads it whole and turns it into a single vector, of 1,024 numbers for the 0.6B
and of 2,560 for the 4B, and the similarity of two excerpts is the cosine of
their vectors. BM25 reads the same text as the lowercase words it contains. No
instruction, title or law name is added for any of the three, and an article
longer than the window of a model, as happens to a handful of very long
articles, is cut at that window.

Two kinds of excerpt are not compared at all, neither as the excerpt being
matched nor as the text it is matched to. The first is the heading, such as the
chapter heading above, and the second is the transitory article, which repeats
the standard wording of a decree, such as the first of the Chapingo law,
**PRIMERO.-** Esta Ley entrará en vigor a los quince días de la fecha de su
publicación en el "Diario Oficial" de la Federación. The preamble and the
closing text, on the other hand, are compared. A third kind is matched but not
counted, and it is a text that several instruments share word for word. Article
56 of the *CÓDIGO Civil Federal* is of this kind, since its text, which reduces
to the label **ARTICULO 56.-** of an article with no body, is exactly the text
of article 56 of the *LEY Federal de Responsabilidades de los Servidores
Públicos*, of the *LEY General de Población* and of the *LEY Orgánica de la
Administración Pública Federal*, so that the match says nothing about any one of
them.

The Chapingo law accordingly has 28 excerpts, which are 16 numbered articles, 5
transitory articles, 5 headings (its four chapters and the heading of the
transitory articles), the preamble and the closing text. The 5 headings and the
5 transitory articles are not compared, and the remaining 18 count, as the
example below shows.

## An example

The two examples below describe the map as it opens, which is drawn from the
0.6B model, so that a reader who has switched to the 4B or to BM25 may see
slightly different numbers in the panel. The *LEY que crea la Universidad
Autónoma Chapingo* has 28 excerpts, 18 of which count, the other ten being
headings and transitory articles that are not compared. For 10 of them the
closest text outside the law belongs to the *LEY Orgánica de la Universidad
Autónoma Metropolitana*, for 6 to the *LEY Orgánica de la Universidad Autónoma
Agraria Antonio Narro*, one goes to the *LEY Orgánica del Instituto Politécnico
Nacional*, and the last one to a treaty, the *CONVENIO INTERNACIONAL PARA EL
ESTABLECIMIENTO DE LA UNIVERSIDAD PARA LA PAZ Y CARTA DE LA UNIVERSIDAD PARA LA PAZ
(MULTILATERAL, 1980)*. On the map the law sits among the organic laws of Antonio
Narro, the UNAM, the UAM and the IPN. The relation is directed, since 21
excerpts of other instruments have their closest text in Chapingo's law, 7 of
them in Antonio Narro's and 7 in the UAM's.

The Constitution has 1,328 excerpts, but only its 136 articles and its
preamble are compared, so that 137 count. Its closest instrument is the *LEY
General de Instituciones y Procedimientos Electorales*, at 14.0. The table
behind that weight lists 14 excerpts, every one a whole 1, among them articles
41, 51 to 56, 58 to 60 and 63 on elections and Congress. The closest of them,
article 96, is matched to article 494 of that law at a similarity of 0.86, and
the weakest, article 58, to its article 10 at 0.67. The next closest
instruments are the *LEY Orgánica del Poder Judicial de la Federación* at 9.0
and the *LEY Orgánica del Congreso General de los Estados Unidos Mexicanos* at
8.0, and a treaty, the *Convención Americana sobre Derechos Humanos*, is among
the five closest at 5.0.

Treaties mostly resemble one another. For 1,284 of the 1,373 treaties the closest
instrument is another treaty, and only 8 laws and 5 regulations have a treaty as
their closest instrument.

## The neighbourhood size

The map is drawn four times from the same data. Each layout is a
two-dimensional UMAP (Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection)
embedding of every instrument's row of weights [@McInnes2018UMAP]. UMAP builds
a graph that joins each point to its nearest neighbours and then lays that
graph out in the plane so that neighbours stay close. The neighbourhood size is
the number of neighbours in that graph, so that small values preserve tight
local groups, such as the universities above, while large values preserve the
overall shape, such as how the laws, the regulations, the guidelines and the
treaties sit relative to one another. Switching it changes the layout and never the
relations listed in the panel.

## The similarity

Two excerpts are close when the method that compares them says so, and the map
can be drawn from any of three methods. Two of them are Qwen3-Embedding models
[@Zhang2025Qwen3Embedding], which turn each excerpt into a list of numbers. The
smaller, Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B (the 0.6B), is the one on which the map opens
and the one that the examples above describe, and the larger,
Qwen3-Embedding-4B (the 4B), is a model of the same family. The third, BM25
[@Robertson2009BM25], is a lexical baseline and not a model at all. It ranks
texts by the words they share, weighting each word by how rare it is among the
excerpts being compared, so that it knows nothing beyond the corpus itself and
does not match an excerpt with a differently worded one that means the same.
Its scores are not on a scale from 0 to 1, and the table behind each weight
therefore calls them scores and shows one decimal.

Choosing another method is not a change of view like the neighbourhood size.
A different method finds different closest texts, so the instruments listed in
the panel, the weights and the lines all change, and the layout is drawn again
from them. The selected instrument stays selected and the neighbourhood size
stays where it was. The map of the 4B or of BM25 is fetched the first time it
is chosen, and the table behind each weight is then read for that method.

## Checking the map against known links

The three methods agree on the closest instrument for most instruments, but
agreement is not correctness, and a method that all three share could be wrong
in the same way. The corpus itself offers a way to check, because an
instrument often says which other instrument it develops, applies or amends.
A regulation exists to develop one law and usually says so, a law may be
reglamentaria of an article of the Constitution, and a treaty may be the
protocol of an earlier one. Such a statement is a strong link between two
instruments that no similarity method was used to find, and it can be used as a
gold standard against which the three data sets are scored.

### How the strong links are built

A strong link goes from one instrument to another, and nothing restricts what
the two are. Every one of the 2,676 instruments on the map can be the source
of a link and every one can be its target, whichever collection each belongs
to, under a single rule, which is that an instrument is never linked to
itself. When two
instruments carry exactly the same name, as the two *LEY de Amnistía* do, or
as a regulation of the Senate does with the law it was filed beside, the name
is the instrument's own and it is not read as a mention of the other.

The links come from three signals, each read from the text of the source. The
first, A, is the name of the instrument. When the name of a regulation contains
the name of a law, as in the *REGLAMENTO DE LA LEY FEDERAL DE CORREDURÍA
PÚBLICA*, the law is the *Ley Federal de Correduría Pública*. The same reading
links a law to the instrument it regulates, the *LEY de Amparo, Reglamentaria
de los artículos 103 y 107 de la Constitución Política de los Estados Unidos
Mexicanos* to the Constitution, and a treaty to the one it implements, the
*AVISO POR EL QUE SE DA A CONOCER EL ESQUEMA DE CERTIFICACION QUE LA REPUBLICA
SOCIALISTA DE VIETNAM APLICARA EN EL MARCO DEL TRATADO INTEGRAL Y PROGRESISTA DE
ASOCIACION TRANSPACIFICO* to that treaty. A treaty is often cited by a short
form of its name, so a treaty name of five words or more is also read without
its trailing qualifier and up to its first comma, and the name of an instrument
that merely extends another with more words is never read as a link to it.
Signal A links 161 instruments: 130 regulations, 19 treaties, 10 laws and two
guidelines. The second, B, is the sentence that states the purpose of the
instrument, usually its first article, which often names what it regulates.
Article 1 of the *REGLAMENTO DE LA LEY DE AGUAS NACIONALES* reads "El presente
ordenamiento tiene por objeto reglamentar la Ley de Aguas Nacionales", which
confirms what its name already said. Article 1 of the *REGLAMENTO DE SISTEMAS DE
COMERCIALIZACIÓN MEDIANTE LA INTEGRACIÓN DE GRUPOS DE CONSUMIDORES* reads "El
presente ordenamiento tiene por objeto regular los sistemas de comercialización
mediante la integración de grupos de consumidores, a que se refiere el artículo
63 de la Ley Federal de Protección al Consumidor", so that its law is found
although its name never mentions it. Signal B links 170 instruments, and the
two signals together link 251 instruments through 275 links.

The links run in many directions, though most of them go from a regulation to a
law. By the collection of the source and of the target, there are 215 links
from regulations to laws, 23 from treaties to treaties, 12 from laws to laws,
nine from guidelines to laws, six from regulations to regulations, five from
regulations to treaties, three from guidelines to regulations and two from laws
to treaties. The 21 treaties that are the source of a link all point to another
treaty, as the *ACUERDO PARA LA APLICACION DE SALVAGUARDIAS EN RELACION CON EL
TRATADO PARA LA PROSCRIPCION DE LAS ARMAS NUCLEARES EN LA AMERICA LATINA Y EL
TRATADO SOBRE LA NO PROLIFERACION DE LAS ARMAS NUCLEARES* does.

A name is not always enough. For 62 instruments the name points to an
instrument that cannot be resolved among the 2,676 of the corpus, as with the
*REGLAMENTO DE LA LEY FEDERAL DE TURISMO*, whose law has been abrogated, and
these instruments are left out of the gold standard instead of being guessed.

The third signal, C, works on single excerpts instead of whole instruments. An
excerpt that cites "artículo 38 Bis de la Ley General del Equilibrio Ecológico
y la Protección al Ambiente" names the instrument it is about, and the same
three data sets can be asked where that instrument ranks for that one excerpt.
The corpus holds 7,066 such citations, in 5,218 distinct excerpts of 1,925
instruments that cite 316 different instruments, once the 258 citations of an
instrument to itself have been set aside. Of those excerpts, 4,497 cite
exactly one instrument. An excerpt that cites two or more instruments is
counted but not scored, because it has no single right answer, and 29 more are
removed because their text is word for word the text of several instruments.
The 4,468 excerpts that remain are scored, and 1,934 of them cite the
Constitution, which every kind of instrument cites. Laws, regulations,
guidelines and treaties all appear among the instruments that cite, and a
treaty cites a law far more often than another treaty, with 863 pairs of an
excerpt and a cited law against 37 of a cited treaty.

### What is measured

At the level of the instrument, each source is scored against its gold
instrument, or its gold instruments when it has several. The panel orders the
other instruments by the weight they receive from the source, which is the
number printed under *Closest instruments*. The measure **closest is a gold
instrument** counts the sources whose gold instrument is the one at the top of
that order, and the measure **a gold instrument among the five closest** counts
those for which a gold instrument is among the first five. The **mean
reciprocal rank** averages, over all the sources scored, the reciprocal rank of
the best-placed gold instrument, which is 1 divided by its position in the
order, so that it is 1 when the instrument is first, 1/2 when it is second and
0 when it receives no weight at all.

At the level of the excerpt, each citing excerpt is compared with the texts of
the 2,675 instruments other than its own. Every one of those instruments is
scored by the similarity of its closest text to the excerpt, and the
instruments are ordered by that score. The rank of the cited instrument is its
position in that order, an instrument whose score only equals the cited
instrument's not being placed ahead of it. The measure **cited instrument
first** is the share of excerpts for which that rank is 1, and the measures
**among the five closest** and **among the ten closest** are the shares for
which it is at most 5 and at most 10. The **mean reciprocal rank** is the
average of 1 divided by the rank, and the **median rank** is the middle value
of the rank over all the excerpts, out of 2,675.

The scores behind these tables are computed by the same three methods and under
the same rules as the map, so that the tables measure the map itself.

Two methods are compared measure by measure, and a single test is used for each
measure. For a measure answered yes or no for every instrument or excerpt, which
are **closest is a gold instrument** and **a gold instrument among the five
closest** at the level of the instrument, and **cited instrument first**,
**among the five closest** and **among the ten closest** at the level of the
excerpt, McNemar's exact test is applied to the cases on which the two methods
disagree, and the difference is real when its p-value is below 0.05. For the
**mean reciprocal rank** and the **median rank**, the difference between the
two methods is given with the 95 % interval of a paired bootstrap, and it is
real when the interval does not contain zero. This rule was fixed before the
results were seen, and when it finds no real difference the two methods are
tied.

### The instruments

The measures below were taken on 12 October 2026, over the 161 instruments of
signal A alone and over the 251 of signals A and B together.

| Gold links | Measure | 0.6B | 4B | BM25 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A (161) | closest is a gold instrument | 102 | 98 | 101 |
| A (161) | a gold instrument among the five closest | 130 | 132 | 132 |
| A (161) | mean reciprocal rank | 0.713 | 0.707 | 0.714 |
| A and B (251) | closest is a gold instrument | 130 | 127 | 129 |
| A and B (251) | a gold instrument among the five closest | 195 | 194 | 193 |
| A and B (251) | mean reciprocal rank | 0.629 | 0.625 | 0.625 |

The methods are then compared two at a time. Each difference is the first method
minus the second, and each cell gives the verdict and, in parentheses, the
p-value of McNemar's test for a measure answered yes or no or the 95 % interval
of the bootstrap for the others.

| Gold links | Pair | closest is a gold instrument | a gold instrument among the five closest | mean reciprocal rank |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A (161) | 0.6B − 4B | tie (p = 0.34) | tie (p = 0.73) | tie ([−0.021, +0.034]) |
| A (161) | 0.6B − BM25 | tie (p = 1.00) | tie (p = 0.75) | tie ([−0.032, +0.031]) |
| A (161) | 4B − BM25 | tie (p = 0.55) | tie (p = 1.00) | tie ([−0.035, +0.020]) |
| A and B (251) | 0.6B − 4B | tie (p = 0.63) | tie (p = 1.00) | tie ([−0.018, +0.026]) |
| A and B (251) | 0.6B − BM25 | tie (p = 1.00) | tie (p = 0.85) | tie ([−0.023, +0.030]) |
| A and B (251) | 4B − BM25 | tie (p = 0.82) | tie (p = 1.00) | tie ([−0.025, +0.024]) |

On what the map shows, which is the closest instrument and the five closest, the
three methods cannot be told apart, and no pair differs on any of the three
measures, on the narrow gold standard or on the wide one. The collection of the
source matters more than the method. Of the 208 regulations scored on the wide
gold standard, the closest instrument is a gold instrument for 122 under the
0.6B and BM25 and for 119 under the 4B, while for the 21 treaties it is so for
five, three and three, and for the 13 laws for none, two and one. The links that
start in a law or a treaty are few, which is why their figures change so much
from one method to the next.

### The excerpts

The same three data sets were then scored one excerpt at a time over the 4,468
excerpts that cite exactly one instrument, and again over the 2,534 excerpts
that remain once those citing the Constitution are set aside.

| Measure | 0.6B | 4B | BM25 |
|---|---|---|---|
| cited instrument first | 0.093 | 0.108 | 0.100 |
| among the five closest | 0.248 | 0.278 | 0.255 |
| among the ten closest | 0.334 | 0.363 | 0.341 |
| mean reciprocal rank | 0.174 | 0.195 | 0.180 |
| median rank | 39 | 30 | 40 |
| among the five closest, without the Constitution | 0.387 | 0.423 | 0.409 |
| mean reciprocal rank, without the Constitution | 0.271 | 0.294 | 0.289 |
| median rank, without the Constitution | 10 | 8 | 9 |

The pairs are compared in the same way, the median rank being given with the
interval of its difference in ranks.

| Pair | cited instrument first | among the five closest | among the ten closest | mean reciprocal rank | median rank |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.6B − 4B | 4B better (p < 0.001) | 4B better (p < 0.001) | 4B better (p < 0.001) | 4B better ([−0.027, −0.016]) | 4B better ([+6, +11]) |
| 0.6B − BM25 | tie (p = 0.09) | tie (p = 0.27) | tie (p = 0.29) | tie ([−0.013, +0.001]) | tie ([−5, +3]) |
| 4B − BM25 | tie (p = 0.08) | 4B better (p < 0.001) | 4B better (p < 0.001) | 4B better ([+0.008, +0.022]) | 4B better ([−14, −6]) |

At this level the methods are no longer tied. The 4B is better than the 0.6B on
all five measures and better than BM25 on four of them, the exception being the
share of excerpts whose cited instrument is first, on which the two cannot be
told apart, and the 0.6B and BM25 are tied on every measure. The differences are
small, two to three points of recall, but they are not noise. The absolute level
is low because an excerpt that cites an article of a law is usually about
something other than the rest of that law, and the Constitution, which is cited
by 1,934 of the excerpts, drags it down further. The order of the three is the
same without the Constitution.

The level depends on who cites. The cited instrument is among the five closest
for 35 %, 41 % and 38 % of the 1,528 excerpts of laws under the 0.6B, the 4B and
BM25, for 26 %, 28 % and 26 % of the 1,901 excerpts of regulations, and for 32 %,
35 % and 28 % of the 185 excerpts of guidelines. For the 854 excerpts of treaties
it is 2.7 %, 2.3 % and 1.9 %, with a median rank above 1,400 in every method. A
treaty that cites an article of a Mexican law mentions it in passing, inside an
agreement about something else, so that the law's own text is probably far from
the excerpt, and none of the three methods bridges that gap.

### The reading

On the question the map answers, which is what an instrument is closest to,
the three methods are indistinguishable at finding the instrument that another
one develops, and a lexical baseline that learns nothing is as good as either
embedding model. The 4B ranks a cited instrument higher for a single excerpt,
and this is the one measured reason for switching to it. BM25 is not beaten
everywhere. Among the ten most cited instruments it is the best on the *Código
Fiscal de la Federación*, where the cited instrument is among the five closest
for 79.7 % of the 172 excerpts against 44.2 % for the 4B, and the lowest of the
three on the Constitution, with 5.2 % of 1,934 excerpts against 8.8 % for the
4B. These checks look at the instrument and not at the article, so they say
nothing about whether the right article of that instrument ranks first.

::: {.atlas-data}
**Data.** The texts are the four consolidated corpora this project publishes
from the Supreme Court (SCJN), namely the [laws](leyes.ipynb)
([`scjn-leyes`](https://github.com/INGEOTEC/LegalIA/releases/tag/scjn-leyes)),
the regulations
([`scjn-reglamentos`](https://github.com/INGEOTEC/LegalIA/releases/tag/scjn-reglamentos))
the guidelines
([`scjn-lineamientos`](https://github.com/INGEOTEC/LegalIA/releases/tag/scjn-lineamientos))
and the treaties
([`scjn-tratados`](https://github.com/INGEOTEC/LegalIA/releases/tag/scjn-tratados)).
They are divided into excerpts and embedded with `Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B`,
the default of the map, and with `Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-4B`, to which the
similarity control switches, as it does to BM25, a lexical baseline computed
from the same excerpts. Of the 203,324 excerpts, 31,172 are headings and 26,182
are transitory articles, neither of which is compared, and 1,947 are
word-for-word texts shared by several instruments, which are matched but not
counted, so that 144,023 count. The map
is a UMAP projection with the cosine metric of each instrument's matches. The
Diario Oficial de la Federación remains the official source of legal text. Map
data generated on <span data-atlas-generated>12 October 2026</span>.

*Read more.* The division of instruments into excerpts is described in
[`md2akn`](https://legalia.readthedocs.io/en/latest/md2akn_api.html), the way
the vectors are read back in
[`legalvec`](https://legalia.readthedocs.io/en/latest/legalvec_api.html), and
the full tables of the two evaluations in the
[project's notes](https://github.com/INGEOTEC/LegalIA/blob/master/scripts/embeddings/README.md).
:::

another instrument and from signal B when the sentence that states the purpose
of the instrument names it, and the full table of links is given below.
